summary: Lists requirements for Emergency Telecommunication Service (ETS) in the context of IP telephony. It extends the general requirements in RFC 3689 and presents no solutions. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3690 lists what IP telephony needs in order to support emergency calling. It says the signalling must carry a marker saying a call is an emergency call, that the marker must be able to hold many different kinds of label, and that the labels should map to the ones the telephone network already uses. It also says the network must be able to treat such calls better than ordinary calls, without saying how.

questions: what is ets in ip telephony
subtitle: What IP telephony must do so that emergency calls are marked and treated as such

tldr.problem: Emergency calls work because the telephone network marks them and gives them special treatment. IP telephony had no equivalent, and a call that crosses between the telephone network and the Internet would lose that marking.
tldr.mechanism: The document lists five requirements on the signalling side of IP telephony: signalling must carry labels, the labels must be extensible, they should map to the emergency markings of other networks, application layer mechanisms must not prevent accounting, and gateways that recognise emergency labels must be able to offer better than best effort service.
tldr.outcome: It defines no solutions at all. It is a requirements list that extends the general Emergency Telecommunications Service requirements of RFC 3689, and it leaves the how to later documents.

facts.label: Excluded from scope
facts.value: IP layer mechanisms such as Differentiated Services and Integrated Services

today: RFC 3690 is an Informational memo published in February 2004, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the general requirements of RFC 3689 to IP telephony and leaves the solutions to later documents.

sections.title: Why Emergency Service Needs Its Own Requirements
sections.content:
Effective telecommunications capabilities can be imperative for immediate recovery operations after serious disaster events such as hurricanes, floods, earthquakes and terrorist attacks. Disasters happen unexpectedly, at any time or place, and a quick response for recovery operations requires immediate access to any public telecommunications capabilities at hand. Those capabilities include the conventional telephone, cellular phones, and Internet access through online terminals, IP telephones and wireless Personal Digital Assistants. Because the commercial telecommunications infrastructure is rapidly moving to Internet-based technology, the Internet community needs to consider how it can best support emergency management and recovery operations.

Other standards bodies have worked on emergency communications. Some of those standards, such as T1.631, define specific indicators or labels for emergency communications in Signalling System 7 networks. Requirements have to be defined so that peering works across hybrid networks, networks that communicate between IP and other types of network such as the Public Switched Telephone Network, and so that the services interwork.
sections.plainLanguage: In the telephone network an emergency call is marked, and the marking is what makes the call get through and get treated properly. When a call travels over both networks, that marking has to survive the boundary, and the requirements for that are what this document lists.

sections.title: Scope and What Is Left Out
sections.content:
RFC 3689 has defined a set of general system requirements to support Emergency Telecommunications Service. This document defines an additional set of system requirements for the specific context of IP telephony, viewing IP telephony as an end-to-end application layer service. Solutions to the requirements are not defined, and the document does not specify protocol enhancements or specifications.

The document notes that RFC 3487, Requirements for Resource Priority Mechanisms for the Session Initiation Protocol, shares some overlap with it, but that RFC 3487 applies only to SIP and is not meant to be applied to the more general question of IP telephony as it relates to emergency service.

One item is deliberately out of scope: mandating acceptance and support of these requirements. The IETF does not mandate requirements or capabilities on the independent networks that make up the Internet. An internet service provider may choose not to operate any telephony-related gateways or services, and the IETF cannot require one to deploy either. The expectation is that business contracts, for example service level agreements, will satisfy the requirements that apply to service providers, and that the absence of such an agreement implies best effort service. It is assumed that some providers will offer emergency service and others will not, and these requirements do not apply to those that have chosen not to offer it.
sections.plainLanguage: The document is a list of requirements, not a design. It is also explicit that nobody is forced to offer emergency calling over IP: a provider that does not offer it is not breaking any rule here.

sections.title: The Five IP Telephony Requirements
sections.content:
The requirements relate only to telephony signalling as used in Internet-based telephony services, and they extend the general requirements of RFC 3689. They explicitly do not relate to IP layer mechanisms such as Differentiated Services or Integrated Services.

  1. Telephony signalling applications used with Internet-based telephony MUST be able to carry labels.
  2. The ability to carry labels MUST be extensible to support various types and numbers of labels. A single binary value will not be sufficient, given the various labelling standards in existence today.
  3. Telephony signalling labels SHOULD have a mapping with the emergency related labels and markings used in other telephony based networks, such as the Public Switched Telephone Network. This ensures that a call placed over a hybrid infrastructure, traditional PSTN over part of the path and Internet telephony over another part, can carry the labels end to end with translation at the boundaries. Absence of a mapping means the signalling reverts to a default service, presumably one attributed to the general public.
  4. Application layer IP telephony capabilities MUST NOT preclude the ability to do application layer accounting. Accounting is a useful feature in support of billing and tracking down abuse of service.
  5. Application layer mechanisms in gateways and stateful proxies that are specifically in place to recognise emergency type labels MUST be able to support best available service, which will probably be realized as better than best effort. These labels MAY exist in the application layer headers of data, that is bearer, traffic or in signalling traffic used for call completion. The support for best available service SHOULD focus on the probability of forwarding packets, which MAY reach 100 percent depending on the local policy associated with the label, and local policy MUST also be used to determine whether better than best effort is applied to a specific label or related set of labels.

The document is careful about how the fifth requirement is read. The paragraphs must be taken in their entirety. The ability to support best available service does not mean that the application layer mechanism is expected to be activated, the means by which best available service is realized are not defined, and application layer mechanisms that do not recognise emergency type labels are not subject to the requirement at all.
sections.plainLanguage: Five things are required of the signalling side of IP telephony: it must carry a label, the label must be able to hold many different things, it should correspond to the emergency markings used elsewhere, it must not stop the network from keeping billing records, and the equipment that recognises emergency labels must be able to treat those calls better than ordinary ones.

sections.title: Issues: Alternate Paths and Best Available Service
sections.content:
The issues section raises matters that arise when looking for solutions to the requirements, and it is not to be confused with requirements.

On alternate paths, experience with the Government Emergency Telecommunications Service over the PSTN has shown the utility of alternate paths to a destination for emergency communications. From the point of view of the Internet, this utility may be harder to achieve and more limited. Unlike the PSTN, which creates a fixed path during call setup, the Internet uses dynamic routing for IP packets, which automatically sends packets along the best current path. The Internet network infrastructure has no concept of a call or of call setup, although IP telephony applications may have application layer awareness of calls.

On the application of best available service, the scope of support is constrained to the application layer and the flows that traverse it. This may involve direct support for the flow carrying the emergency label, or indirect support, for example emergency labels in signalling messages that cause an effect on the corresponding data or bearer flows. How the support is realized, and how effective a given approach or implementation turns out to be, are both outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Two problems are left open. The telephone network can set up a second route to the emergency centre, and the Internet cannot easily do that. And the document says how much better than ordinary service an emergency call should get, without saying how to arrange it.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
Only authorised users or operators SHOULD be able to create non-ordinary labels, that is, labels that may alter the default best effort service. Labels SHOULD be associated with mechanisms that provide strong end-to-end integrity during their transmission through the telephony systems. Where labels are expected to be acted upon by operators, those operators SHOULD have the capability of authenticating the label on a received message or transmission, in order to prevent theft of service and to reduce the risk of denial of service, for example by unauthorised users consuming limited resources.

Security is also discussed in the general requirements of RFC 3689, which apply to the requirements in section 3.
sections.plainLanguage: Because a label can buy a call better treatment, only authorised people should be able to create one, the label should be protected against alteration while it travels, and the operator should be able to check who created it.

items.title: Carry labels
items.text: Telephony signalling applications used with Internet-based telephony must be able to carry labels.

items.title: Make labels extensible
items.text: The ability to carry labels must be extensible to support various types and numbers of labels, since a single binary value will not be sufficient.

items.title: Map to other networks
items.text: Labels should have a mapping with the emergency labels used in other telephony networks, so a call over a hybrid path keeps them end to end.

items.title: Keep accounting possible
items.text: Application layer capabilities must not preclude application layer accounting, which supports billing and tracking down abuse of service.

items.title: Support best available service
items.text: Mechanisms that recognise emergency labels must be able to support best available service, with local policy deciding whether it applies.
